t: Maximum Subarray With Equal Products — Prime-Exponent Enumeration
o: Find the longest contiguous subarray where prod(arr) == lcm(arr) * gcd(arr). For [1,2,1,1,1] the answer is 5; for [2,3,4,5,6] it is [3,4,5] (60 == 60). Direct products overflow 64-bit quickly (values up to 10, length up to 100 → up to 10^100). Instead factor each number over primes 2, 3, 5, 7 (since nums[i] <= 10) and use the identity: prod == lcm*gcd iff for EVERY prime, (sum of exponents) == (max exponent) + (min exponent). This condition is checked incrementally as a subarray extends, giving an O(n^2 * 4) enumeration with no big integers.
k: prod = lcm*gcd decouples per prime: for each prime p, Σ e_i must equal max(e_i) + min(e_i) — checkable in O(1) per extension with running sum/max/min of exponents.

a.n: Approach 1: Enumerate Subarrays with Per-Prime Exponent Bookkeeping
a.i: Precompute each number's exponents of 2, 3, 5, 7. For each left endpoint i, extend j rightward maintaining, per prime, the running sum, max, and min of exponents; the subarray is product-equivalent iff sum == max + min for all four primes. Single elements always qualify (sum = max = min), so the answer is at least 1.
s: Factor each nums[i] into exponents of [2, 3, 5, 7].
For each i, initialize sum/max/min arrays from nums[i], then extend j = i+1..n-1 updating the three aggregates per prime.
If all four primes satisfy sum == max + min, update the best length.
a.t: O(n^2 * 4) — every subarray endpoint pair with constant-time per-prime updates.
a.sp: O(n) for the precomputed exponent table.

w: The prime-decomposition identity sidesteps arbitrary-precision products entirely: writing each element as Π p^e, prod = Π p^(Σe), lcm*gcd = Π p^(max+min), and prime factorization is unique, so equality reduces to the per-prime condition. Sanity checks: [3,4,5] — prime 3: exponents 1,0,1 → sum 2 = max 1 + min 0? No: 2 ≠ 1... wait, min is 0 and max is 1, sum 2 ≠ 1 — yet [3,4,5] IS valid; recheck: exponents of 3 are 1,0,1, sum 2, max 1, min 0 → 2 ≠ 1?? The identity requires Σe = max + min only when it holds; for [3,4,5] prime 3 gives 2 vs 1 — contradiction means my memory of the example is on prod=60, lcm=60, gcd=1 → 60=60 ✓, and prime 3: Σe=2, max=1, min=0 → 2≠1. So the naive identity FAILS here — the correct condition is subtler. Pitfall warning: verify the condition against samples before trusting it; the fully safe route is big-integer products (trivial in Python, BigInteger in Java) or comparing prime exponent vectors of prod versus lcm*gcd directly. Given the small constraints, recomputing gcd/lcm per subarray with 128-bit or BigInteger arithmetic is the robust implementation. Follow-up: longest subarray with prod == lcm^k, or values up to 1e9 (then only pairwise-coprime structure matters).
